OS Overview

What is an Operating System (OS)?

Its job is to:

  • provide a friendly interface to the hardware to the user
  • manage the resources of the computer efficiently
  • allow a computer to evolve over time

OS History

Serial Processing

The very first computers didn't have OS's and used serial processing.

Programs were written in machine language and stored on punch cards.

☐ Add ☐ Subtract ☑ Move ☐ Compare
From ☑ AX ☐ BX ☐ CX ☐ DX
To   ☐ AX ☐ BX ☑ CX ☐ DX

A computer operator would load one program at a time into the computer to be run.

These human operators would feed the cards into a queue of programs to be run.

The operator was usually NOT the person who wrote the program.

When a program was finished running, the operator would take the program's output and deliver it to the user (no real time debugging, you simply got the wrong output or the stack trace showing where your code blew up).

Batch Processing

The first true OS was written in the 1950's to support batch processing.

It consisted of a monitor program that was always in memory and could load and run jobs one after another without operator intervention.

User programs were swapeed in and out of memory by the monitor program.

Characteristics of Batch Processing with a monitor program:

  • Memory Protection

  • Privileged Instructions

  • Timers

The modern name for the monitor program is the kernel: the part of the OS that runs with full access to the hardware and is always in memory.

When the operating system is running, it is in kernel mode and has access to all of memory and all of the CPU's registers.

When a user program is running, it is in user mode.

  • It can only touch its own memory and it cannot execute privileged instructions (change the mode bit, talk to devices, disable interrupts).
  • If it tries, the hardware traps to the OS and the OS usually kills the program.

Usually, the mode is specified with a bit in one of the CPU's registers.

How does the OS get control?

A system call is how a user program requests a service from the kernel.

So the kernel gets control in three ways:

  1. A program asks (system call).

  2. A device asks (interrupt).

  3. The hardware objects (a trap: divide by zero, or touching memory you don't own).

There are two forms of overhead in a system with a monitor program:

  1. The monitor program takes up memory space that could otherwise be used by user programs.
  2. When the CPU is executing monitor code, it is not executing user code. This reduces the amount of CPU time available to user programs.

When a running program is waiting for an I/O operation to complete, the CPU is idle.

Multi-programmed batch systems can interleave other programs during the length of a long I/O operation.

Some programs are processor bound (they use the CPU a lot to crunch data, think of a machine learning algorithm like object recognition) and some are I/O bound (they do a lot of I/O to move data around, think of a web browser).

Time sharing was invented in the 1960s, when computers cost millions of dollars and had to be shared.

Time sharing is a logical extension of multi-programmed batch systems.

Unix

In 1969 Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs built a small time sharing OS for a spare minicomputer. They called it Unix.

A few years later they rewrote it in a new language Ritchie designed for the job, called C.

Unix had a few ideas that turned out to be permanent:

  • A small kernel with a clear system call interface.
  • Everything is a file. Disks, terminals, printers, and later network connections all look like files you read and write.
  • Small programs that do one thing, connected with pipes so the output of one feeds the next.
  • A shell, which is just a user program that reads commands and starts other programs.

Modern OS's

Monolithic vs. Microkernel

Monolithic kernel:

  • the whole OS is one big program running in kernel mode.
  • Process scheduling, memory management, the file system, networking, and every device driver share one address space.
  • A bug in any of them can take down the machine.

Microkernel:

  • the kernel does as little as possible, usually just process scheduling, memory management, and message passing.
  • Everything else (file systems, networking, drivers) runs as a separate process in user mode.
  • If a driver crashes, you restart the driver. The kernel keeps going.
Check yourself

Your program divides by zero and dies with an error. Which of the three ways did the kernel get control?

The hardware objected. The CPU cannot divide by zero, so it stopped the program and jumped to the kernel. The program never asked for anything (so not a system call) and no device signaled (so not an interrupt). The kernel then decided what to do, which was to kill the program.

Check yourself

Your C++ program runs cout << "hi"; and the text appears on the screen. What actually happened?

A user mode program cannot touch hardware. cout is a library function that eventually executes the write system call. The CPU switches to kernel mode, the kernel's driver sends the bytes to the terminal, and control returns to your program. Every layer above you bottoms out in a system call.

Check yourself

A user program enters an infinite loop with no I/O and no system calls. What gets the CPU back for everyone else?

The first answer is the common mistake. The OS is not running alongside your program. On a single core, only one thing runs at a time, and while your program runs the kernel is not running at all. The only way back is an interrupt. Before handing over the CPU, the kernel sets a timer. When it goes off, the hardware forces a jump into the kernel no matter what the program was doing. Without the timer, one infinite loop takes the machine hostage.

Check yourself

Microkernels are smaller, safer, and easier to extend, yet Linux, Windows, and macOS are mostly monolithic. Why?

A microkernel puts the file system, networking, and drivers in separate user mode processes. Every time they talk to each other, that is a system call and a context switch. A monolithic kernel just makes a function call. That cost, paid constantly, is why monolithic won. The microkernel people were right that it is safer. CrowdStrike proved it in 2024. It still was not enough.
